subject: physics
title: Measurements & Uncertainties Adventure 2: Random vs systematic errors
welcome_lead: Today you'll separate random from systematic errors in measurement.
meta_desc: Physics — random vs systematic errors, precision vs accuracy, repeats, zero error.
final_note: You learned random errors scatter (reduce with means), systematic errors shift (need calibration), precision ≠ accuracy.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Random: equally likely too high or low. Sources: reaction time, fluctuations, last-digit estimation.
Reduce by taking more repeats and averaging.

Systematic: same direction always. Sources: zero error, faulty calibration, parallax, heat loss.
Cannot be reduced by repeats — must find + fix cause.

- Precise + accurate: tight cluster near bullseye.
- Precise but inaccurate: tight cluster, off-target (systematic).
- Imprecise but accurate: scattered around bullseye (random).
- Neither: scattered off-target.

A stuck stopwatch is precise but inaccurate.

Take repeats of the same measurement:

- Standard deviation ≈ random error.
- Mean offset from accepted value ≈ systematic error.

Always quote uncertainty: e.g. (5.34 ± 0.05) cm. The uncertainty must have only 1 sig fig (occasionally 2).
